claim: Avian takeoff requires peak pectoralis muscle power to generate sufficient aerodynamic force during the downstroke.
source: Avian takeoff requires peak pectoralis muscle power to generate sufficient aerodynamic force during the downstroke.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle of avian flight mechanics.

claim: The supracoracoideus recovers the wing during the upstroke.
source: Subsequently, the much smaller supracoracoideus recovers the wing during the upstroke.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of the supracoracoideus muscle.

claim: Doves reduce the angle of attack of their wing mid-downstroke to efficiently generate aerodynamic force.
source: Doves reduce the angle of attack of their wing mid-downstroke to efficiently generate aerodynamic force, resulting in an aerodynamic power dip, that allows transferring excess pectoralis power into tensioning the supracoracoideus tendon to assist the upstroke—improving the pectoralis work loop efficiency simultaneously.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the results.

claim: The mid-downstroke reduction in angle of attack results in an aerodynamic power dip.
source: Doves reduce the angle of attack of their wing mid-downstroke to efficiently generate aerodynamic force, resulting in an aerodynamic power dip, that allows transferring excess pectoralis power into tensioning the supracoracoideus tendon to assist the upstroke—improving the pectoralis work loop efficiency simultaneously.
evidence: This causal relationship is stated in the abstract and demonstrated with data in Figure 4A.

claim: The aerodynamic power dip allows transferring excess pectoralis power into tensioning the supracoracoideus tendon to assist the upstroke.
source: Doves reduce the angle of attack of their wing mid-downstroke to efficiently generate aerodynamic force, resulting in an aerodynamic power dip, that allows transferring excess pectoralis power into tensioning the supracoracoideus tendon to assist the upstroke—improving the pectoralis work loop efficiency simultaneously.
evidence: This mechanism is proposed based on modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Tensioning the supracoracoideus tendon improves the pectoralis work loop efficiency.
source: Doves reduce the angle of attack of their wing mid-downstroke to efficiently generate aerodynamic force, resulting in an aerodynamic power dip, that allows transferring excess pectoralis power into tensioning the supracoracoideus tendon to assist the upstroke—improving the pectoralis work loop efficiency simultaneously.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling in Figure 5, showing improved work loop shape factors.

claim: Birds with faster wingtip speed need to generate proportionally more pectoralis power.
source: Integrating extant bird data, our model shows how the pectoralis of birds with faster wingtip speed need to generate proportionally more power.
evidence: This scaling relationship is derived from modeling and shown in Figure 7A and C with Equation 1.

claim: Birds with disproportionally larger wing inertia need to activate the pectoralis earlier to tune their downstroke.
source: Finally, birds with disproportionally larger wing inertia need to activate the pectoralis earlier to tune their downstroke.
evidence: This is derived from scaling analysis and shown in Figure 7B and D with Equations 2 and 3.

claim: During slow flight, negligible lift is induced by forward body motion.
source: During slow flight, negligible lift is induced by forward body motion, so instead, almost all the aerodynamic force is generated by the flapping motion of the wings.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle of slow flight aerodynamics.

claim: Almost all aerodynamic force during slow flight is generated by the flapping motion of the wings.
source: During slow flight, negligible lift is induced by forward body motion, so instead, almost all the aerodynamic force is generated by the flapping motion of the wings.
evidence: This follows from the negligible contribution of forward motion during slow flight.

claim: Slow flight is one of the most energetically expensive modes of locomotion.
source: Hence, slow flight is one of the most energetically expensive modes of locomotion (Altshuler and Dudley, 2003; Ellerby and Askew, 2007; Tobalske et al., 2003; Heers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In generalist birds, the pectoralis is the largest muscle in the avian body.
source: Furthermore, in generalist birds, the downstroke muscle, the pectoralis, is of primary importance energetically: it is the largest muscle in the avian body.
evidence: This is stated as an anatomical fact about generalist birds.

claim: The pectoralis is 3–5 times larger than the supracoracoideus.
source: It is 3–5 times larger than the next largest wing muscle, the supracoracoideus, which controls the upstroke (Tobalske and Biewener, 2008).
evidence: This size comparison is supported by citation to Tobalske and Biewener, 2008.

claim: The supracoracoideus controls the upstroke.
source: It is 3–5 times larger than the next largest wing muscle, the supracoracoideus, which controls the upstroke (Tobalske and Biewener, 2008).
evidence: This functional role is stated with citation support.

claim: The pectoralis has a broad origin with a complex arrangement of muscle fibers.
source: However, the pectoralis has a broad origin with a complex arrangement of muscle fibers, making global measurement of muscle fiber strain challenging.
evidence: This anatomical description explains experimental challenges.

claim: The complex arrangement of pectoralis muscle fibers makes global measurement of muscle fiber strain challenging.
source: However, the pectoralis has a broad origin with a complex arrangement of muscle fibers, making global measurement of muscle fiber strain challenging.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological challenge in the field.

claim: The current state-of-the-art recordings in birds measure muscle length changes with sonomicrometry.
source: The current state-of-the-art recordings in birds measure muscle length changes with sonomicrometry (Biewener et al., 1998; Soman et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes the current methodological standard with citations.

claim: To measure muscle stress, the state-of-the-art solution is to attach a strain gauge to the deltopectoral crest (DPC).
source: To measure muscle stress, the state-of-the-art solution is to attach a strain gauge to the deltopectoral crest (DPC), which is located where the pectoralis inserts on the humerus (Tobalske et al., 2003; Tobalske and Biewener, 2008; Biewener et al., 1992; Biewener et al., 1998; Dial and Biewener, 1993).
evidence: This describes the current methodological standard with multiple citations.

claim: The deltopectoral crest is located where the pectoralis inserts on the humerus.
source: To measure muscle stress, the state-of-the-art solution is to attach a strain gauge to the deltopectoral crest (DPC), which is located where the pectoralis inserts on the humerus (Tobalske et al., 2003; Tobalske and Biewener, 2008; Biewener et al., 1992; Biewener et al., 1998; Dial and Biewener, 1993).
evidence: This is an anatomical fact stated with citations.

claim: Pull calibrations to correlate bone strain to muscle stress are complicated by multiple factors.
source: However, pull calibrations to correlate bone strain to muscle stress are complicated by multiple factors.
evidence: This introduces methodological limitations in prior work.

claim: Misalignment between the changing pull axis of the muscle in vivo and the pull axis of the force transducer post mortem is a source of skew in calibrations.
source: One source of skew is misalignment between the changing pull axis of the muscle through the stroke in vivo and the pull axis of the force transducer used for the pull calibration post mortem (Tobalske and Biewener, 2008), which was refined by Jackson and Dial, 2011a.
evidence: This methodological issue is described with citations to prior work.

claim: The supracoracoideus has pennate muscle fibers attached to a long tendon.
source: It has pennate muscle fibers attached to a long tendon, making it better suited for producing force than work, which would facilitate storing and releasing significant amounts of elastic energy in the supracoracoideus tendon (Biewener and Baudinette, 1995; Roberts et al., 1997; Biewener, 1998; Biewener and Roberts, 2000).
evidence: This anatomical description is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The pennate fiber architecture of the supracoracoideus makes it better suited for producing force than work.
source: It has pennate muscle fibers attached to a long tendon, making it better suited for producing force than work, which would facilitate storing and releasing significant amounts of elastic energy in the supracoracoideus tendon (Biewener and Baudinette, 1995; Roberts et al., 1997; Biewener, 1998; Biewener and Roberts, 2000).
evidence: This functional interpretation is based on muscle architecture principles with citations.

claim: The supracoracoideus architecture facilitates storing and releasing significant amounts of elastic energy in the supracoracoideus tendon.
source: It has pennate muscle fibers attached to a long tendon, making it better suited for producing force than work, which would facilitate storing and releasing significant amounts of elastic energy in the supracoracoideus tendon (Biewener and Baudinette, 1995; Roberts et al., 1997; Biewener, 1998; Biewener and Roberts, 2000).
evidence: This functional consequence is inferred from anatomy with citation support.

claim: Measurements in pigeons suggest elastic storage in the supracoracoideus may range between 28 and 60% of the net work of the supracoracoideus.
source: Measurements in pigeons (Columba livia) suggest this elastic storage may range between 28 and 60% of the net work of the supracoracoideus (Tobalske and Biewener, 2008), which is thought to primarily elevate and supinate the wing.
evidence: This quantitative estimate is based on measurements cited from Tobalske and Biewener, 2008.

claim: The supracoracoideus is thought to primarily elevate and supinate the wing.
source: Measurements in pigeons (Columba livia) suggest this elastic storage may range between 28 and 60% of the net work of the supracoracoideus (Tobalske and Biewener, 2008), which is thought to primarily elevate and supinate the wing.
evidence: This functional role is stated as current understanding with citation.

claim: The supracoracoideus is used in every flight mode.
source: However, while the supracoracoideus is used in every flight mode (Dial, 1992; Tobalske, 1995), birds are still able to fly without its use (Degernes and Feduccia, 2001; Sokoloff et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior research.

claim: Birds are still able to fly without use of the supracoracoideus.
source: However, while the supracoracoideus is used in every flight mode (Dial, 1992; Tobalske, 1995), birds are still able to fly without its use (Degernes and Feduccia, 2001; Sokoloff et al., 2001).
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The study focused on the second downstroke after takeoff during level flight in ringneck doves.
source: We focused on the second downstroke after takeoff during level flight in ringneck doves (Streptopelia risoria; hereafter 'doves') because it was the first downstroke that well supported bodyweight after takeoff.
evidence: This describes the experimental design choice.

claim: The second downstroke after takeoff was the first downstroke that well supported bodyweight after takeoff.
source: We focused on the second downstroke after takeoff during level flight in ringneck doves (Streptopelia risoria; hereafter 'doves') because it was the first downstroke that well supported bodyweight after takeoff.
evidence: This justifies the choice of which stroke to analyze.

claim: During the second wingbeat, there is a dip in the angle of attack during the middle of the downstroke when peak aerodynamic force is generated.
source: During the second wingbeat, there is a dip in the angle of attack during the middle of the downstroke when peak aerodynamic force is generated.
evidence: This is a primary finding shown in Figure 2C and Figure 3A.

claim: The mid-downstroke dip in angle of attack coincides with a peak in the power factor.
source: This dip coincides with a peak in the power factor (non-dimensional lift3/2 to drag ratio), which hence lessens the aerodynamic power required to generate lift.
evidence: This relationship is demonstrated in Figure 3C.

claim: The peak in power factor lessens the aerodynamic power required to generate lift.
source: This dip coincides with a peak in the power factor (non-dimensional lift3/2 to drag ratio), which hence lessens the aerodynamic power required to generate lift.
evidence: This is inferred from the definition of power factor and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: During the downstroke, the first peak in angle of attack (54.0° ± 5.0°) is reached after 7.1% of the stroke.
source: During the downstroke, the angle of attack across the span of the wing (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) starts and ends with peaks with a valley in-between: the first peak (54.0° ± 5.0°) is reached after 7.1% of the stroke and the second peak (68.4° ± 12.1°) is reached at 49.4% of the stroke (which corresponds to 10.9% before the end of the downstroke), with a large dip (30.5° ± 3.1°) in the middle at 27.7% of the stroke.
evidence: This quantitative measurement is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The second peak in angle of attack (68.4° ± 12.1°) is reached at 49.4% of the stroke.
source: During the downstroke, the angle of attack across the span of the wing (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) starts and ends with peaks with a valley in-between: the first peak (54.0° ± 5.0°) is reached after 7.1% of the stroke and the second peak (68.4° ± 12.1°) is reached at 49.4% of the stroke (which corresponds to 10.9% before the end of the downstroke), with a large dip (30.5° ± 3.1°) in the middle at 27.7% of the stroke.
evidence: This quantitative measurement is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The mid-downstroke dip in angle of attack (30.5° ± 3.1°) occurs at 27.7% of the stroke.
source: During the downstroke, the angle of attack across the span of the wing (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) starts and ends with peaks with a valley in-between: the first peak (54.0° ± 5.0°) is reached after 7.1% of the stroke and the second peak (68.4° ± 12.1°) is reached at 49.4% of the stroke (which corresponds to 10.9% before the end of the downstroke), with a large dip (30.5° ± 3.1°) in the middle at 27.7% of the stroke.
evidence: This quantitative measurement is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The mid-downstroke dip in angle of attack corresponds with a mid-downstroke dip in wing drag.
source: Our aerodynamic force recordings show this dip in mid-downstroke angle of attack corresponds with a mid-downstroke dip in wing drag and peak in net aerodynamic force (Figure 3B).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The mid-downstroke dip in angle of attack corresponds with a peak in net aerodynamic force.
source: Our aerodynamic force recordings show this dip in mid-downstroke angle of attack corresponds with a mid-downstroke dip in wing drag and peak in net aerodynamic force (Figure 3B).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The power factor peak (timing after start of downstroke: 29.8% of the stroke) corresponds to the mid-downstroke angle of attack dip.
source: Comparing the angle of attack (Figure 2C) with the power factor (Figure 3C) of the doves during the downstroke, the power factor peak (timing after start of downstroke: 29.8% of the stroke) corresponds to the mid-downstroke angle of attack dip.
evidence: This temporal correspondence is demonstrated by comparing Figure 2C and Figure 3C.

claim: The second peak in drag after the mid-downstroke dip is larger than the first peak (maximum drag scaled by bodyweight before mid-downstroke dip: 0.92 ± 0.22; after: 1.60 ± 0.46).
source: Of the two peaks in drag (Figure 3B), the second peak after the mid-downstroke dip is larger (maximum drag scaled by bodyweight before mid-downstroke dip: 0.92 ± 0.22; after: 1.60 ± 0.46).
evidence: This quantitative comparison is based on data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The larger second drag peak is caused by two factors: the corresponding angle of attack is higher and the wing area is larger.
source: This is caused by two factors: the corresponding angle of attack is higher and the wing area is larger.
evidence: This explanation is inferred from the data in Figures 2C and 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The dove primarily uses lift for weight support (stroke-averaged vertical aerodynamic force scaled by bodyweight for lift: 66.17% ± 10.81%; drag: 22.11% ± 4.62%).
source: Examining the directional components of lift and drag (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we find the dove primarily uses lift for weight support (stroke-averaged vertical aerodynamic force scaled by bodyweight for lift: 66.17% ± 10.81%; drag: 22.11% ± 4.62%).
evidence: This quantitative breakdown is based on data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The secondary function of lift is to overcome drag (stroke-averaged horizontal aerodynamic force scaled by bodyweight for lift: 32.84% ± 9.96%; drag: –27.64% ± 4.64%).
source: The secondary function of lift is to overcome drag (stroke-averaged horizontal aerodynamic force scaled by bodyweight for lift: 32.84% ± 9.96%; drag: –27.64% ± 4.64%).
evidence: This quantitative breakdown is based on data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Drag primarily points backward throughout the downstroke, and laterally at the beginning and end of the downstroke.
source: Drag primarily points backward throughout the downstroke, and laterally at the beginning and end of the downstroke (the lateral forces of the wings cancel).
evidence: This directional description is based on data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lateral forces of the wings cancel.
source: Drag primarily points backward throughout the downstroke, and laterally at the beginning and end of the downstroke (the lateral forces of the wings cancel).
evidence: This is inferred from bilateral symmetry of the wings.

claim: Both lift and drag contribute to weight support during takeoff.
source: Due to the small peaks in drag before and after the mid-downstroke dip, drag contributes to weight support at the beginning and end of the downstroke, so both lift and drag contribute to weight support during takeoff.
evidence: This is inferred from the directional components shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: During the upstroke the dove folds its wings inward.
source: Finally, during the upstroke the dove folds its wings inward (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), producing very little aerodynamic force (scaled by bodyweight vertically: 11.28% ± 2.81%; horizontally: 2.68% ± 1.49%).
evidence: This kinematic observation is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: During the upstroke, the dove produces very little aerodynamic force (scaled by bodyweight vertically: 11.28% ± 2.81%; horizontally: 2.68% ± 1.49%).
source: Finally, during the upstroke the dove folds its wings inward (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), producing very little aerodynamic force (scaled by bodyweight vertically: 11.28% ± 2.81%; horizontally: 2.68% ± 1.49%).
evidence: This quantitative measurement is based on aerodynamic force data.

claim: For doves, aerodynamic power is dominant during the downstroke.
source: Aerodynamic power dominates during the downstroke, whereas inertial power dominates the upstroke (Figure 4B; Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For doves, inertial power dominates the upstroke.
source: Aerodynamic power dominates during the downstroke, whereas inertial power dominates the upstroke (Figure 4B; Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Inertial power evens out the two peaks in aerodynamic power adjacent to the mid-downstroke dip.
source: However, we observe inertial power evens out the two peaks in aerodynamic power adjacent to the mid-downstroke dip (peak in aerodynamic + inertial power scaled by pectoralis mass before mid-downstroke dip: 537.0 ± 221.5 W/kg; after: 580.0 ± 176.8 W/kg; minimum dip: 455.0 ± 287.0 W/kg).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing aerodynamic power alone to aerodynamic plus inertial power in Figure 4B.

claim: The difference in aerodynamic power peaks is 206.1 ± 248.3 W/kg.
source: Whereas for the aerodynamic power, the difference in the peaks is 206.1 ± 248.3 W/kg, with the addition of inertial power the difference in peaks reduces to 43.0 ± 283.4 W/kg.
evidence: This quantitative comparison is based on data analysis.

claim: With the addition of inertial power, the difference in peaks reduces to 43.0 ± 283.4 W/kg.
source: Whereas for the aerodynamic power, the difference in the peaks is 206.1 ± 248.3 W/kg, with the addition of inertial power the difference in peaks reduces to 43.0 ± 283.4 W/kg.
evidence: This quantitative comparison demonstrates the smoothing effect of inertial power.

claim: A power increase of 24.9% ± 17.5% in the pectoralis muscle would enable it to fully power the upstroke by tensioning the supracoracoideus tendon during the downstroke.
source: We find that a power increase of 24.9% ± 17.5% in the pectoralis muscle would enable it to fully power the upstroke by tensioning the supracoracoideus tendon during the downstroke.
evidence: This is derived from the muscle-tendon model shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The pectoralis would need to generate 206.0 ± 49.6 W/kg (stroke-averaged positive power scaled by pectoralis mass) if no energy was stored in the supracoracoideus tendon.
source: The pectoralis would need to generate 206.0 ± 49.6 W/kg (stroke-averaged positive power scaled by pectoralis mass) if no energy was stored in the supracoracoideus tendon.
evidence: This is calculated from the model shown in Figure 5B.

claim: An increase of 24.9% ± 17.5% power generation in the pectoralis (to 255.9 ± 62.7 W/kg) would allow the supracoracoideus tendon to store enough elastic energy to fully power the upstroke.
source: At the other extreme, an increase of 24.9% ± 17.5% power generation in the pectoralis (to 255.9 ± 62.7 W/kg) would stretch the tendon of the supracoracoideus and allow it to store enough elastic energy to fully power the upstroke.
evidence: This is calculated from the model shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Applying a storage fraction of 28–60% as measured in Tobalske and Biewener, 2008 requires only an increase in pectoralis work of between 6.8 and 14.5%.
source: Applying a storage fraction of 28–60% as measured in Tobalske and Biewener, 2008 to our model requires only an increase in pectoralis work of between 6.8 and 14.5%.
evidence: This is calculated by applying literature values to the model.

claim: Elastic storage in the supracoracoideus tendon is an effective solution to help power the upstroke that simultaneously smoothes the mid-stroke power output of the pectoralis.
source: Hence, elastic storage in the supracoracoideus tendon appears to be an effective solution to help power the upstroke that simultaneously smoothes the mid-stroke power output of the pectoralis.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the modeling results in Figure 5.

claim: Short storage time results in a spike in pectoralis power near the end of the downstroke, which produces a low pectoralis work loop shape factor (0.49 ± 0.14).
source: Short storage time (Figure 5C) results in a spike in pectoralis power near the end of the downstroke, which produces a low pectoralis work loop shape factor (the actual loop area divided by the potential maximum area for the observed peak force and length change: 0.49 ± 0.14; Figure 5E and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5C and quantified in Figure 5G.

claim: When the storage time is appropriately spread out over the downstroke, the pectoralis work loop shape factor increases to a maximum value of 0.73 ± 0.11.
source: On the other hand, when the storage time is appropriately spread out over the downstroke (Figure 5D), the pectoralis work loop shape factor increases to a maximum value of 0.73 ± 0.11.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5D and quantified in Figure 5G.

claim: A shape factor of over 0.72 ± 0.11 can be achieved for any energy storage over 35%.
source: While this maximum shape factor is achieved when the energy storage in the supracoracoideus tendon equals 90%, a shape factor of over 0.72 ± 0.11 can be achieved for any energy storage over 35% (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: For any energy storage over 35%, the maximum shape factor corresponds to a storage time of 31% of the stroke.
source: For any energy storage over 35%, the maximum shape factor corresponds to a storage time of 31% of the stroke.
evidence: This is derived from analysis of Figure 5—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Storing energy in the supracoracoideus tendon for 31% of the stroke has the effect of flatting out the mid-downstroke pectoralis power generation and improving the shape factor.
source: Hence, storing energy in the supracoracoideus tendon for 31% of the stroke has the effect of flatting out the mid-downstroke pectoralis power generation and improving the shape factor.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results in Figure 5.

claim: Tensioning the supracoracoideus tendon is key for proper wing stroke kinematics.
source: Since a mid-contraction dip in power generation is unnatural for muscles, tensioning the supracoracoideus tendon is key for proper wing stroke kinematics: instead of the wing continuing to accelerate mid-downstroke when velocity peaks, the wing reaches zero acceleration at this point, after which it decelerates to prepare for stroke reversal.
evidence: This is inferred from muscle mechanics principles and kinematic observations.

claim: During downstroke, the pull angle computed for doves in slow flight is lower than chukars during wing-assisted incline running.
source: During downstroke, the pull angle that we compute for the doves in slow flight (black line) is lower than chukars during wing-assisted incline running (Heers et al., 2016) (gray line).
evidence: This comparison is shown in Figure 6C with citation to Heers et al., 2016.

claim: If pectoralis moment is used to tension the supracoracoideus tendon during the second half of the downstroke, the pull angle would increase to values higher than plotted and shift towards chukar values.
source: However, if pectoralis moment is used to tension the supracoracoideus tendon during the second half of the downstroke to more finely tune the wingbeat, the pull angle would necessarily increase to values higher than plotted here and shift the curve towards chukar values.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model and comparison with chukar data.

claim: The mid-downstroke angle of attack of doves (30.5° ± 3.1°) is especially pronounced compared to other species.
source: The dove's mid-downstroke dip in the angle of attack (to 30.5° ± 3.1°), which has a cascading effect on drag, aerodynamic power, and energy storage, is especially pronounced compared to other species.
evidence: This comparison is made with literature values for other species.

claim: In Pacific parrotlets the mid-downstroke angle of attack is higher, roughly between 45° and 60°.
source: For example, in Pacific parrotlets (Forpus coelestis) the mid-downstroke angle of attack is higher, roughly between 45° and 60° (Deetjen et al., 2017), under similar takeoff conditions for the second wingbeat.
evidence: This comparison is based on citation to Deetjen et al., 2017.

claim: In barn owls flying at higher speeds after takeoff, the angle of attack mid-downstroke is roughly 30° at 5–6 m/s flight speed.
source: In contrast, in barn owls (Tyto alba) flying at higher speeds after takeoff, the angle of attack mid-downstroke is lower, roughly 30° at 5–6 m/s flight speed (Wolf and Konrath, 2015).
evidence: This comparison is based on citation to Wolf and Konrath, 2015.

claim: The advance ratio of the doves during takeoff is 0.14 ± 0.01.
source: A comparison with hovering birds is more representative because the advance ratio (ratio of forward flight speed to wingtip speed) of the doves during takeoff is 0.14 ± 0.01, which is close to hovering (advance ratio < 0.1; Ellington, 1984).
evidence: This is measured data shown in Table 2.

claim: The angle of attack of hovering hummingbirds is 36.9° ± 4.9° during mid-downstroke.
source: The angle of attack of the doves is most similar to that of hovering hummingbirds, whose angle of attack is 36.9° ± 4.9° (across n = 88 individuals from 17 species) during mid-downstroke, with peaks at the beginning (51.3° ± 10.9°) and end (52.7° ± 9.9°) of the downstroke (Ingersoll et al., 2018), so the mid-downstroke dip is flatter for hummingbirds.
evidence: This comparison is based on citation to Ingersoll et al., 2018.

claim: The average mid-downstroke angle of attack in hovering bats is 52.2° ± 5.0°.
source: In contrast, the average mid-downstroke angle of attack in hovering bats is 52.2° ± 5.0° (across n = 16 individuals from two nectar and one fruit bat species, of which the latter has the highest angle of attack; Ingersoll et al., 2018).
evidence: This comparison is based on citation to Ingersoll et al., 2018.

claim: The bat's angle of attack trace shape is more similar to that of doves than hummingbirds.
source: Notably the bat's angle of attack trace shape is more similar to that of doves.
evidence: This is a qualitative comparison based on literature data.

claim: The current study calculated an average net pectoralis power of between 182 ± 48 W/kg (no energy storage) and 232 ± 60 W/kg (full energy storage) for doves flying at 1.23 ± 0.13 m/s.
source: We calculated an average net pectoralis power of between 182 ± 48 W/kg (no energy storage) and 232 ± 60 W/kg (full energy storage) for doves flying at 1.23 ± 0.13 m/s, meaning that, based on our measurements, Tobalske et al., 2003 underestimated the pectoralis power by between 1.6% ± 26.6% (no elastic storage) and 29.4% ± 33.3% (elastic storage fully powers upstroke), which is small in comparison to the variance among other studies.
evidence: This is calculated from the model and data.

claim: Tobalske et al., 2003 reports an average net pectoralis power of 179 W/kg for doves flying at 1 m/s.
source: The only comparable study for doves is Tobalske et al., 2003, which reports an average net pectoralis power of 179 W/kg for doves flying at 1 m/s.
evidence: This is cited from Tobalske et al., 2003.

claim: Based on the current measurements, Tobalske et al., 2003 underestimated the pectoralis power by between 1.6% ± 26.6% (no elastic storage) and 29.4% ± 33.3% (elastic storage fully powers upstroke).
source: We calculated an average net pectoralis power of between 182 ± 48 W/kg (no energy storage) and 232 ± 60 W/kg (full energy storage) for doves flying at 1.23 ± 0.13 m/s, meaning that, based on our measurements, Tobalske et al., 2003 underestimated the pectoralis power by between 1.6% ± 26.6% (no elastic storage) and 29.4% ± 33.3% (elastic storage fully powers upstroke), which is small in comparison to the variance among other studies.
evidence: This comparison is calculated from the current data and literature values.

claim: For any energy storage fraction in the supracoracoideus tendon above 35%, a pectoralis work loop shape factor of over 0.72 ± 0.11 can be achieved if the energy storage is spread out appropriately over the course of the downstroke.
source: We find that for any energy storage fraction in the supracoracoideus tendon above 35%, a pectoralis work loop shape factor of over 0.72 ± 0.11 can be achieved (global maximum of 0.73 ± 0.10) if the energy storage is spread out appropriately over the course of the downstroke (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5F and G.

claim: The global maximum pectoralis work loop shape factor is 0.73 ± 0.10.
source: We find that for any energy storage fraction in the supracoracoideus tendon above 35%, a pectoralis work loop shape factor of over 0.72 ± 0.11 can be achieved (global maximum of 0.73 ± 0.10) if the energy storage is spread out appropriately over the course of the downstroke (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: Work loops from strain-gauge measurements are relatively triangular with a shape factor of 0.62.
source: Compared to work loops previously reported from strain-gauge measurements of muscle stress, which are relatively triangular (data from Tobalske et al., 2003 is plotted in Figure 5E for a dove in similar conditions; shape factor = 0.62; Tobalske et al., 2003; Jackson and Dial, 2011a), our more rectangular work loops suggest an improved generation of work because the relative area of positive work is greater for a rectangle than a triangle with the same maximum stress and strain.
evidence: This comparison is made with data from Tobalske et al., 2003 shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The more rectangular work loops from the current study suggest an improved generation of work compared to triangular work loops.
source: Compared to work loops previously reported from strain-gauge measurements of muscle stress, which are relatively triangular (data from Tobalske et al., 2003 is plotted in Figure 5E for a dove in similar conditions; shape factor = 0.62; Tobalske et al., 2003; Jackson and Dial, 2011a), our more rectangular work loops suggest an improved generation of work because the relative area of positive work is greater for a rectangle than a triangle with the same maximum stress and strain.
evidence: This is inferred from geometric principles of work loops.

claim: In hummingbirds, aerodynamic power is similar during upstroke and downstroke.
source: In contrast, hummingbirds produce a similar amount of aerodynamic power during upstroke and downstroke (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A), and inertial power is dominant throughout the stroke (Figure 7—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A.

claim: In hummingbirds, inertial power is dominant throughout the stroke.
source: In contrast, hummingbirds produce a similar amount of aerodynamic power during upstroke and downstroke (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A), and inertial power is dominant throughout the stroke (Figure 7—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The increased influence of inertia in hummingbirds is likely due to their higher wingbeat frequency (79 Hz) compared to doves (9.8 Hz).
source: The increased influence of inertia is likely due to the higher wingbeat frequency of the hummingbirds (79 Hz; Ingersoll and Lentink, 2018) compared to the doves (9.8 Hz; Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the scaling relationship between frequency and inertial power.

claim: The masses of the pectoralis and supracoracoideus muscles are more similar in hummingbirds (approximately 2:1 ratio) than doves (ratio of 4.60 ± 0.93).
source: Unsurprisingly, the masses of the pectoralis and supracoracoideus muscles are more similar in hummingbirds (approximately 2:1 ratio; Ingersoll and Lentink, 2018) than doves (ratio of 4.60 ± 0.93) because hummingbirds need more total muscle power during the upstroke than doves (Figure 7—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This comparison is based on data from the current study and citation to Ingersoll and Lentink, 2018.

claim: Hummingbirds need more total muscle power during the upstroke than doves.
source: Unsurprisingly, the masses of the pectoralis and supracoracoideus muscles are more similar in hummingbirds (approximately 2:1 ratio; Ingersoll and Lentink, 2018) than doves (ratio of 4.60 ± 0.93) because hummingbirds need more total muscle power during the upstroke than doves (Figure 7—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4C.
